warmup.text: This book starts with a boy who says something no narrator should be able to say. He is a ghost. Then he says he is not a ghost yet. Hold on to both of those. Today you meet Isaac, his family, and his dog Jumper, in the Choctaw Nation in 1830. Keep one question with you: what does Isaac know that you don't?

words.text: Two word parts run through this whole book. One is about remembering. One is about writing. Isaac is doing both. Try to find them before the page tells you. When you get to the river game, say each word slowly and listen for where your voice stops.

reading.text: Read Chapters 1 and 2 in your book. Keep your reading lens in mind as you go. When you finish, do the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

assignment.text: Three questions about the chapters, then the first step of your own writing. When a question asks for evidence, use Isaac's own words. In the Writer's Workshop you are only making a list today. Pick moments you can still feel.

hook.q: On the first page, Isaac guesses what you are wishing for. Would you want to see things before they happen?

options.t: Yes. I'd know what was coming.
options.reply: Lots of readers pick this one. Here is what Isaac says to you:
Isaac would understand. Here is what he says to you:
That would be nice. Isaac doesn't get to choose. Here is what he says to you:

reveal.line: Be careful what you wish for.
reveal.then: Keep that warning in mind as you read Chapters 1 and 2. Watch for the moment his wish comes true.

do: Read the three lenses.
Tap the one you will use today.
Keep it in mind as you read. You will use it at the end.
how.why: Historical fiction mixes real history with a made-up voice. Knowing which is which helps you read both.
how.use: You will use this when you answer the chapter questions.

Read why each one is correct.
Fix the second sentence out loud.
Tap Check My Work to compare.
how.why: A sentence where someone does the action is clearer and stronger to read.

do: Read Group A and Group B.
Think through the question.
Tap See what was hiding to check.
Type the four words, then tap Check My Answers.
how.why: Isaac is remembering and writing his story. These two roots name exactly that.

do: Read the book sentence on each card.
Guess what the word means.
Tap the card to check.
Match each word to its meaning.
how.why: These words show up in this week's chapters. Knowing them first keeps the reading smooth.

do: Read the sentence and the question.
Tap the first word of each appositive.
Answer Show What You Know in the box.
how.why: Writers use appositives to tell you more about a person without starting a new sentence.

Tap Now name the pattern to check yourself.

how.why: Knowing open and closed syllables helps you read long words you have never seen.

Answer each question in 2 or more sentences.
Use Isaac's own words as evidence.
how.why: These questions check that you followed both the history and Isaac's voice.

List 3 or 4 moments in the box.
One line for each moment is enough.
how.why: This week you will write one moment from the inside, the way Isaac does. Today you only choose it.
how.use: Tomorrow you will pick one moment from this list and draft it.

Open your book and read Chapters 1–2.
Then do the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

glossary.meaning: a made-up story set in a real time and place in the past
what was happening around the story: the time, the place, and the events

memoir: It is a kind of book.
It is a memory written down. It starts with mem.
It starts with memo and ends with ir.
manuscript: It is written by hand, before printing.
manu means hand. Add the root that means write.
inscription: It starts with in and has script in the middle.
memorize: What you do to keep something in your memory.
It starts with memor and ends with ize.

miss.native: Say na-tive. The first beat, na, ends on the vowel a, and the a says its name. That makes it open.
miss.choctaw: Say Choc-taw. The first beat, Choc, ends on the consonant c, and the o is short. That makes it closed.
miss.nation: Say na-tion. The first beat, na, ends on a, and the a says its name. That makes it open.
miss.blanket: Say blan-ket. The first beat, blan, ends on n, and the a is short. That makes it closed.
miss.tribal: Say tri-bal. The first beat, tri, ends on i, and the i says its name. That makes it open.
miss.hunting: Say hunt-ing. The first beat, hunt, ends on t, and the u is short. That makes it closed.

game.title: Stones in the River
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 stones today
game.look: In Chapter 3, Isaac remembers a river with sharp stones on the bottom. In this game, the stones help you. Each stone holds a word from Isaac's world: his family's garden, supper table and river. Split the word after its first beat, then say whether that beat is open or closed. Every word you finish lights a stone. Your crossing keeps going all week.

do: Say the word slowly.
Tap the gap where the first beat ends.
Tap Open or Closed.
Tap Next stone.
how.why: This is the same open and closed rule from Spelling, with new words. If you can split a word you have never practiced, you really know the rule.

game.doneLine: Every stone for today is lit. Come back tomorrow for more.

stones.why: Yes. to ends on o, and the o says its name. Open.
Yes. sup ends on p, and the u is short. Closed.
Yes. pa ends on a, and the a says its name. Open.
Yes. fish ends on the sound sh, and the i is short. Closed.
stones.gapHint: Say it slowly: fish... ing. sh makes one sound, so keep s and h together.

stones.why: Yes. na ends on a, and the a says its name. Open.
Yes. din ends on n, and the i is short. Closed.

art.title: Mississippi, a map printed around 1831
art.alt: An old hand-colored map of Mississippi. A large yellow area in the middle is labeled Choctaw Indians.
art.look: This map was printed in Philadelphia around the time of Isaac's story. The big yellow area marked “Choctaw Indians” is the Choctaw Nation, where Isaac's family lives. The small colored blocks in the south are counties the state had already made. A map like this was made by people outside the Choctaw Nation, and it only shows what they chose to draw.
art.creator: Anthony Finley, engraved by Young & Delleker
art.lookBtn: Tap to learn about this map

cards.title: Choctaw words in the book
cards.intro: Isaac tells his story in English, but some Choctaw words stay in it. Here are three you will meet this week.

items.meaning: Okay. Isaac explains it himself in Chapter 1.
items.line: “Hoke,” I said, which means “okay” in Choctaw.

items.meaning: The word Isaac's family uses for the people who are not Choctaw and live nearby. Your vocabulary card gives its meaning: a white person.
items.line: Nahullos were people that lived a few miles away. They were not Choctaws, like us.

items.meaning: Thank you. You will see it on Day 3, in Chapter 6.

cards.note: The narrator does not say these words aloud. Choctaw has its own sounds, and we would rather not teach them wrong.

virtue.name: courage
virtue.title: Courage or not?
virtue.intro: You just read Chapters 1 and 2. Read each moment. Tap Courage or Not courage.

items.t: At the river, Isaac's mother tells him, “Don't talk. Just watch.” Isaac stays and watches, even though it scares him.
items.why: He keeps looking at something hard instead of turning away. That takes courage.

items.t: When Luke hears there is Treaty Talk, he leaves to play stickball with his friends.
items.why: Luke walks away from the hard news. Playing is not wrong, but this moment is not courage.

items.t: Isaac sees Mister Jonah's hair burst into flames. He jerks his arm free from his mother and runs toward him.
items.why: He moves toward danger to help someone. That is courage, even though the flames turn out to be a vision.

items.t: Isaac is afraid of Treaty Talk and does not want to listen anymore. He thinks, maybe it will all go away.
items.why: Wishing a hard thing away is normal, but it is not courage yet. Courage means facing it.
